Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information from the flight plan, FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot input. It consists of Flight Guidance (FG) for pitch and roll commands, an Autopilot (AP) for attitude control, an Autothrottle (AT) for engine thrust control, and Yaw Dampers (YDs) for Dutchroll damping and turning coordination. A Mach Trim system provides horizontal stabilizer trim commands based on Mach changes when the AP is disengaged within a preset Mach range.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time. It is the default vertical mode if no other vertical modes are selected, or if a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode is selected. Engaging the AP also activates PTCH Mode when both FDs are disengaged.

The ALTS Mode is always armed except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. When the vertical Mode is GA, ALTS is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits the ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes.
Deselection of Vertical Speed Mode (VS) occurs when other vertical modes are selected or captured.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.
The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is designed to prevent the aircraft speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed.

The USPD Mode is automatically activated when underspeed occurs, unless ALTS or ALT mode is captured or active. When activated, an amber USPD symbol is displayed and an "underspeed" aural alert is given. Underspeed is defined as airspeed less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach less than Mman - 0.01.

The ALTS Mode is always armed unless the ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. When the vertical Mode is GA, ALTS is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. During altitude capture, ALTS is activated when the new altitude is selected or the current altitude is maintained.
In the VS Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference. The PITCH/VS Wheel is used to change the VS reference.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In the APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.

The OSPD Mode is designed to automatically activate when the aircraft's Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or its airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt, and it generates pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo.

The USPD Mode automatically activates when the aircraft's airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01, unless ALTS or ALT mode is captured or active. It displays an amber USPD symbol and gives an "underspeed" aural alert. The AP and AT provide commands to increase airspeed and prevent stall. The SPEED Knob is inhibited while in USPD Mode, and other vertical modes are inhibited except in ALTS, ALT, TO, and GA modes. AT is armed when in USPD mode. USPD mode automatically deactivates when airspeed/Mach exceeds Vman/Mman, and the system switches to FLC mode with the current altitude reference maintained.
The WS Mode integrates airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data to generate optimal escape maneuver commands. It sets AT to TOGA thrust.

Modes engaged or captured show in green letters at the top of the FMA. Modes armed show in white letters at the bottom of the FMA.

Vertical modes can be deselected by manually selecting other vertical modes, or by changing the FG coupled side (for TO mode). They can also be deselected by selecting other vertical modes or capturing other vertical modes.
Incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
In PTCH Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is always armed except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. It is armed during GA Mode if the preselected altitude is 75 ft above the current altitude. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. ALTS Mode activates during altitude capture when a new altitude is selected or the current altitude is maintained.

The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) is activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or automatically when the preselected altitude changes during ALTS Mode activation or capture. It is also activated when VNAV is deselected in favor of ALTV Mode, or when the FMS altitude is tracked in ALTV Mode. If APPR Mode is engaged during GS capture, ALT Mode is inhibited.

In the VS Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference. The PITCH/VS Wheel is used to change the VS reference, with slow rotation changing it by 100 ft/min per click and quick rotation by more than 100 ft/min per click. The vertical speed reference is limited to ± 8000 ft/min. The VS reference is synchronized to the current VS on the coupled side when the VS Mode is activated, the AP is engaged, or the SYNC Pushbutton is pressed. In VS Mode, the AT controls airspeed.
The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope.

The TO Mode can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side or manually selecting other lateral modes. Pressing the TOGA Pushbutton also deselects the TO Mode. When activated, AP is engaged and TO Mode is cancelled.

The GA Mode can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side, manually selecting other lateral modes, or by pressing the SYNC Pushbutton on either side. When the aircraft is in flight, pressing the TOGA Pushbutton selects the GA Mode.

The OSPD Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft's Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or its airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. It generates pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. Other vertical modes are inhibited unless in ALTS, ALT, TO, or GA Mode. AT is armed in OSPD Mode, and the system returns to FLC Mode when the airspeed is below the limit.

The USPD Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. When the airspeed/Mach exceeds Vman/Mman, USPD mode deactivates automatically and switches to FLC Mode.

The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) automatically switches the lateral mode to GA and the vertical mode to WS when TAWS triggers a windshear warning. It generates optimal escape maneuver commands by integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until the windshear warnings cease. To manually exit WS Mode, any other vertical mode must be selected.

Responses: The Autoflight System manages and controls the aircraft's lateral and vertical flight path using information from the flight plan, FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot inputs. It utilizes two Flight Generators (FG), one Autopilot (AP), one Autothrottle (AT), and three Yaw Dampers (YD) to control pitch, roll, thrust, and damping. Pitch and roll are managed by servo mechanisms, while the AT controls engine thrust based on data from various aircraft systems.
The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.
it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
The FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is always armed, except when the ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. When the vertical Mode is GA, the ALTS Mode is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP will inhibit the ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes.
In the VS Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In the APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.
The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is designed to prevent the aircraft speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode automatically activates when the aircraft's airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01, unless ALTS or ALT mode is captured or active. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. The mode deactivates automatically when airspeed/Mach exceeds Vman/Mman, and the airspeed reference is set to Vman + 5 kt/Mman +0.01. During USPD, the SPEED Knob is inhibited, and other vertical modes are generally inhibited unless in ALTS, ALT, TO, or GA Mode. AT is armed when USPD is active.
The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) commands a nose up pitch of 15° or below the Alpha Margin Indicator (AMI), whichever is lower. If the Autothrottle (AT) is engaged, it is set to TOGA thrust.

The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) is activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP), or automatically when the preselected altitude changes during ALTS Mode capture or when the VNAV Mode is deselected.

The Vertical Speed (VS) Mode is selected by pressing the VS Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). Its function is to hold a preselected vertical speed. This mode is inhibited if the APPR Mode is in vertical capture or tracking, or if the aircraft is in OSPD Mode.

The FLC Mode holds airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent. It controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed. The FLC Mode generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed, to achieve preselected target altitude. When holding the airspeed/Mach reference or the minimum vertical speed, the FG generates a greater closure rate to reach the target altitude.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In the APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.
The TO Mode is activated and can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side or manually selecting other lateral or vertical modes. It can be engaged by pressing the TOGA Pushbutton.

The GA Mode is activated by pressing the TOGA Pushbutton. It can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side or manually selecting other lateral or vertical modes. When activated, pitch angle is commanded in accordance with the go-around target speed. The pitch control upper limit of the Autopilot remains at 20°, while the Flight Director's pitch control upper limit expands to 30°.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or the airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. Its function is to generate pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The speed reference in OSPD Mode is Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01, unless ALTS or ALT mode is active. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman to prevent stall. The SPEED Knob is inhibited when USPD Mode is active. USPD Mode deactivates automatically when the airspeed/Mach is greater than Vman/Mman, at which point the airspeed reference is set to Vman + 5 kt/Mman + 0.01, the FG vertical Mode switches to FLC Mode, and the current altitude reference remains. AP does not disengage but reverts to arm. Other vertical modes are inhibited unless in ALTS Mode, ALT Mode, TO Mode, and GA Mode. AT is armed when USPD Mode is active.

The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) is automatically entered when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. It provides optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data. The system automatically switches the lateral Mode to GA and the vertical Mode to WS. The AP disengages automatically after 2 seconds. AT is set to TOGA thrust. To manually exit WS Mode, another vertical mode must be selected once the windshear warning ceases.

Responses: The Autoflight System controls the aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust.
The Autoflight System controls pitch and roll via the pitch servo and roll servo, respectively, and thrust via the AT servo.
The AT Modes are integrated with the various vertical/lateral modes and the flight management system.
During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
Selecting other vertical modes deselects the current vertical mode and captures a new one.
When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
The basic vertical Mode of the Autoflight System is PTCH. In the PTCH Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is always armed except when the ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. If the vertical Mode is GA, the ALTS Mode is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP will inhibit the ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude change. During altitude capture, the ALTS Mode is activated when the new attitude is selected or the current altitude is being maintained.
In the ALT Mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to acquire and maintain the current pressure altitude.
The Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference.

The FLC Mode generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed, to achieve a preselected target altitude. When holding the airspeed/Mach reference or the minimum vertical speed, the FG generates a greater closure rate to reach the target altitude.

VNAV Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for vertical modes, automatically selecting ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the flight plan's vertical constraints.

The APPR Mode, when active, generates commands in the lateral axis to track and capture the selected navigation source (FMS/LOC/VOR). For precision approaches, it also activates the related vertical Mode when armed.

The TO Mode provides pitch guidance of 15° for two-engine operation and 12° for one-engine operation after liftoff, until the aircraft speed reaches the takeoff target speed (V2+ 10 kt). It also activates FDs on both sides, sets the AT to takeoff thrust, and expands the pitch command upper limit of the FD to 30°. The TO Mode can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side or manually selecting other lateral or vertical modes.
The GA Mode is activated.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft Mach number is more than Mmo + 0.01, or the airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. It generates pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman to prevent stall stick shaker.

The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) provides optimal escape maneuver commands by integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until windshear warnings cease. The system automatically switches to GA lateral mode and WS vertical mode when TAWS triggers a windshear warning. The AT is set to TOGA thrust in WS Mode.

The ALT Mode can be activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or automatically when the preselected altitude changes during ALTS Mode activation or capture. It can also be activated when VNAV Mode is deselected in favor of ALTV Mode, or when the FMS altitude is tracked in ALTV Mode. The ALT Mode is deselected by pressing the ALT Button.
Pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or activating other vertical modes.

Responses: The Autoflight System controls the aircraft's pitch and roll commands using two Flight Guides (FGs) and two Flight Directors (FDs). The Autopilot (AP) uses pitch and roll servo mechanisms to control the aircraft's attitude based on FG guidance. The Autothrottle (AT) receives data from various sources including FGs and the Flight Management System (FMS) to provide automatic thrust control commands. Three Yaw Dampers (YDs) are also part of the system, providing Dutchroll damping and turning coordination. Additionally, a Mach Trim system generates horizontal stabilizer trim commands based on Mach changes when the AP is disengaged and the aircraft is within a preset Mach range.
The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.
During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
When a vertical Mode is selected, the incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
In PTCH Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is always armed unless ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. If GA Mode is active, ALTS is armed if the preselected altitude is 75 ft above the current altitude. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. When ALTS Mode is active, the FG commands capture or follow the preselected barometric altitude. If VNAV is not engaged, the FCP ALT knob sets the altitude reference. If VNAV is engaged, the FMS target altitude can also be used, and the FG uses the altitude closest to the aircraft. The AT controls airspeed in ALTS Mode. ALTS Mode deselects if ALT, GS, or GA Mode is activated.
In Vertical Speed Mode (VS), the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the preselected vertical speed.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope.
The OSPD Mode is designed to prevent the aircraft speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo by generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed. The speed reference in this mode is Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt.

The USPD Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. The speed reference is Vman + 5 kt or Mman + 0.01 when the mode deactivates automatically.

The Autoflight System provides windshear recovery guidance by sending calculated pitch and roll maneuver commands. After the TAWS sends a windshear warning, the FD will first send a nose up command of 15° or below the Alpha Margin Indicator (AMI), whichever is lower. The AT is set to TOGA thrust in WS Mode. After the windshear condition disappears, the command bar is 15° or slightly below AMI pitch attitude, whichever is lower.

Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft.
The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo and AT servo.
The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.
it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
When a vertical Mode is selected, incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is the basic vertical Mode of the Autoflight System. In this mode, the Flight Guidance (FG) generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the time the mode is selected.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode generates commands to capture or follow the preselected barometric altitude reference. If VNAV is not engaged, it uses the altitude set on the ALT Knob. If VNAV is activated, it can use the FMS target altitude as well, prioritizing the closest altitude to the aircraft or the FCP preselected altitude if they match. The AT controls airspeed in ALTS Mode. ALTS Mode is armed unless ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. It is inhibited if the ALT knob is rotated. It deselects when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is activated. During ALT capture or when ALTS is engaged and the preselected altitude changes, ALT mode will be active, and the new preselected altitude becomes the reference.
The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) is activated to acquire and maintain the current pressure altitude.

The Vertical Speed (VS) Mode is selected by pressing the VS Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). In this mode, the Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the preselected vertical speed reference. The PITCH/VS Wheel is used to change this reference.

The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed. It generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed, to achieve preselected target altitude. When holding the airspeed/Mach reference or the minimum vertical speed, the FG generates a greater closure rate to reach the target altitude.

Once VNAV is active, FMS can automatically select the vertical Mode as required. It will automatically select ALTS, ALT, VS or FLC based on the vertical constraints of the flight plan, and provide the altitude and speed references in these Modes.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope.

The TO Mode is activated when the TOGA Pushbutton is pressed on the ground. After aircraft liftoff, it provides pitch guidance of 15° for two-engine operation and 12° for one-engine operation until the aircraft speed reaches the takeoff target speed (V2+ 10 kt). It also activates the FDs on both sides and sets the AT to takeoff thrust. The pitch command upper limit of the FD expands to 30°, while the AP's pitch control upper limit remains at 20°.

The Go-around (GA) Mode can be selected by pressing the TOGA Pushbutton when the aircraft is in flight. In this mode, the Autopilot System provides commands to hold the current heading laterally, with a bank angle limit of ±5°. Vertically, it commands pitch to achieve the go-around target speed, with an initial lower limit pitch angle of 8° that can reduce to 4°. The pitch command upper limit for the Flight Director expands to 30°, while the Autopilot's pitch control upper limit remains at 20°. The go-around target speed is the greater of VAPP or current speed, ranging from VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 20 kt during two-engine operation, and VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 15 kt during single-engine operation. The GA Mode can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side, manually selecting other lateral or vertical modes, or by pressing the SYNC Pushbutton. The FMA displays "GA" in green when this mode is activated. The Automatic Takeoff Thrust Control System (ATTCS) is also automatically engaged during the Go-Around Phase.

The OSPD Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft's Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01, or its airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. Its function is to generate pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. The SPEED Knob is inhibited when OSPD Mode is active.

The USPD Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. Its function is to generate pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. When the current airspeed/Mach is greater than Vman/Mman, USPD mode deactivates automatically and the airspeed reference is set to Vman + 5 kt/Mman + 0.01. The SPEED Knob is inhibited when USPD Mode is active.

The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) is automatically entered when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. The Autoflight System then provides windshear recovery guidance by sending calculated pitch and roll maneuver commands to the Flight Director (FD). The Autopilot (AP) disengages automatically after 2 seconds. The system generates optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data. To manually exit WS Mode, another vertical mode must be selected. In WS Mode, Autothrottle (AT) is set to TOGA thrust.

Responses: The FMS Operations - Advanced Flight Plan chapter covers the creation and deletion of waypoints, changes to the flight plan, parallel offsets, holding patterns, operations in high latitudes, and alternate airport procedures.

The FMS Operations - Advanced Flight Plan chapter details various methods for adding waypoints, including inserting waypoints directly on the LEGS page, creating pilot-defined waypoints such as Along-Track Offset (ATO) and Place Bearing/Distance (PBD) waypoints, and adding direct-to waypoints via the ACT/MOD FPLN page. Discontinuities are used to show a break in a flight plan sequence and to keep a changed portion of a flight plan isolated from an unchanged portion during certain edits or changes.

Discontinuities can be deleted using a DELETE command from the scratchpad, or by inserting the next applicable waypoint at the discontinuity prompts. However, some discontinuities cannot be deleted with the DEL key, such as those before an approach with an initial radar-vectored leg, at the end of an airway where the next waypoint is not on that airway, or before a leg without a defined starting point (e.g., a DME-arc leg).
When a discontinuity is deleted, a Direct-To course is created to the next waypoint in the flight plan.

Responses: The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft. It controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust.
The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo and AT servo.
The vertical Mode, lateral Mode and AT Mode show on the FMA at the top of the PFD.
During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP).
When a vertical Mode is selected, incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.
The basic vertical Mode of the Autoflight System is PTCH. In the PTCH Mode, the FG generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at Mode selection.

The ALTS Mode is always armed unless ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. When the vertical mode is GA, ALTS is armed if the preselected altitude is 75 ft higher than the current altitude. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. The ALTS Mode is activated during altitude capture or when maintaining the current altitude. It generates commands to capture or follow the preselected barometric altitude. The Autopilot controls airspeed in ALTS Mode.
The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) acquires and maintains the current pressure altitude when selected. The Autothrottle (AT) controls airspeed in this mode.
The Autoflight System generates commands to maintain the VS reference.

The FLC Mode controls pitch to maintain a commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed. It generates commands to hold the selected airspeed/Mach or the minimum vertical speed to achieve the preselected target altitude, generating a greater closure rate to reach that altitude.

VNAV Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for altitude and speed constraints. It can automatically select other vertical modes like ALTS, ALT, VS, or FLC based on the flight plan's vertical constraints.

The APPR Mode is a lateral mode that allows the Autoflight System to track and capture the selected navigation source (FMS/LOC/VOR) during an approach. For precision approaches, when APPR Mode is armed, the related vertical mode is activated. The system operates in the active lateral mode (HDG or NAV) until the aircraft is in a position to intercept the final approach course.

The Takeoff (TO) Mode is activated by pressing the TOGA Pushbutton on the ground. After lift-off, it provides pitch guidance of 15° for two-engine operation or 12° for one-engine operation until the aircraft reaches the takeoff target speed. The Autothrottle (AT) is set to takeoff thrust, and the Flight Director (FD) activates on both sides. The pitch command upper limit of the FD expands to 30°, but the Autopilot (AP) pitch control upper limit remains at 20°. It can be deselected by changing the FG coupled side or manually selecting other lateral or vertical modes.
Guidance is based on go-around target speed.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is automatically activated when the aircraft Mach number is more than Mmo + 0.01, or the airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. It generates pitch commands to reduce the airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. In both modes, the Autopilot (AP) reverts to an armed state (white ARM on the FMA), and the Autothrottle (AT) is armed.

The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) is automatically entered when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. The system generates optimal escape maneuver commands by integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data. These commands continue until windshear warnings cease. To manually exit, another vertical mode must be selected. The Autothrottle (AT) is set to TOGA thrust in WS Mode.
The ALT Mode acquires and maintains the current pressure altitude when selected.
The ALT Mode can be deselected by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP), which changes the vertical mode to PTCH, or by activating other vertical modes.

Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when conditions change. The TAU for a TA is about 40 seconds.

Resolution Advisory (RA) is a real collision threat with a TAU of about 25 seconds. It provides aural messages and displays orders on the PFD to maintain the current V/S (preventive resolution advisory - PRA) or modify V/S (corrective resolution advisory - CRA).

Indication is displayed as a filled red box on the vertical speed scale of the PFD, and an aural alert will sound. It indicates the relative altitude or absolute altitude of the traffic with units of 100 ft. An arrow indicates if the traffic is climbing or descending.

Responses: TCAS detects aircraft in its vicinity, displays potential and predicted collision targets, and issues vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflict.
TCAS is independent of the ground-based ATC.
The TCAS detection capability is limited to intruders flying within a maximum lateral range of 30 NM – 40 NM and within a maximum altitude range of 9900 ft (9900 ft above/below the aircraft).
The display can indicate up to 30 aircraft simultaneously.
The TCAS has one TCAS receiver/transmitter and two TCAS directional antennas.
TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders. Depending on the replies, TCAS determines for each intruder its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude.
Its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude.
Then the TCAS computes the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA.
When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered.

TCAS classifies intruders into the following levels: Proximate traffic (no collision threat), Traffic Advisory (TA - potential collision threat), Resolution Advisory (RA - real collision threat), and Other Traffic (no collision threat, optional display).
Proximate traffic is displayed as a filled cyan diamond.
Traffic Advisory (TA) is a warning of proximate traffic that may become a threat when conditions change. The Time to closest approach (TAU) for a TA is about 40 seconds.
It is displayed as a filled amber circle and an aural alert will sound.
Resolution Advisory (RA) is a warning of a real collision threat with a TAU of about 25 seconds.

RAs are displayed as a filled red box on the PFD/MFD and on the vertical speed scale of the PFD. They provide aural alerts and indicate the relative altitude or absolute altitude of the traffic with units of 100 ft. The color of the altitude matches the color of the traffic symbol. An arrow indicates if the traffic is climbing or descending.
The two types of vertical orders for an RA are Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA) and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).
Other Traffic is non-threat traffic. It can be optionally displayed. When displayed, it appears as a filled cyan diamond.
Traffic Advisory (TA), Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA), and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).
It informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when the conditions change.
To avoid deviation from the present vertical flight path.
that maintaining the present path will resolve the threat situatio
arns the pilot to take actions ( such as climb or descent ) to avoid threat aggravation.

TCAS alerts are inhibited below 1100 ft AGL during climb or below 900 ft AGL during descent. They are also inhibited below 1200 ft AGL during climb or below 1000 ft AGL during descend. There are two modes of pressure refueling: automatic refueling and manual refueling.
The refueling mode is selected using the REFUEL SELECTION Switch on the Refuel/Defuel Control Panel.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to AUTO. The INCR/DECRT Switch is used to set the required refuel quantity. The Refuel Shutoff Valve is manually selected open to start refueling. The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the refueling process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when fuel in the tank reaches the preselected quantity. Once the fuel quantities are balanced, both refuel shutoff valves are opened to complete the refueling process simultaneously.

Under manual refueling mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set in MANUAL. The refueling personnel can open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch on the Refuel/defuel Control Panel. The manual shutoff function overrides the automatic shutoff function.

Responses: PACKs, mixing manifold, recirculation filters, recirculation fans, outflow valve, and integrated air system controllers.

Bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted by flow control valves and then enters the PACKs. Within the PACK, bleed air is cooled through a primary heat exchanger, compressed by an air cycle machine compressor, further cooled in a main heat exchanger, and then passed through a reheater/condenser. It then goes through a high-pressure water separator, expands and cools, before being delivered to the mixing manifold.

The air conditioning system and its components are controlled and monitored by two Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs). The IASCs also regulate the flow control valves for bleed air shutoff, overheat protection, and temperature regulation.
When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft.
When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.

The emergency RAM air function provides adequate fresh air to the cockpit and cabin by allowing outside air to enter the mixing manifold through the emergency RAM air valve. This is activated by the flight crew using the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel, but only when both PACKs have failed, the flight altitude is below 10000 ft, and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
The flight crew can open the emergency RAM air valve with the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.
The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans, and then it is distributed to the cabin through the distribution duct.
Emergency RAM air valve and low pressure ground connectio
Ground air conditioning sourc

Two recirculation fans are used for air recirculation in the cabin. They extract air from the lower side of the cabin, filter it, and send part of it to the mixing manifold and the rest to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
check valves installed on the recirculation fa
The RECIRC Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel controls the recirculation fans. Integrated air system controllers can only passively monitor their status.
Integrated air system controllers can only passively monitor the status of the recirculation fans but not control them.

The trim air system adds hot air to the distribution duct leaving the mixing manifold to adjust the temperature of the cockpit and cabin independently according to their different temperature requirements.
Manually selecting the TRIM Switch OFF closes the valves disabling the trim air system.
The trim air pressure regulating valve adjusts the air pressure entering the trim air duct from downstream of the flow control valve. When it is closed, the trim air system is inoperative.
The trim air pressure regulating valve is pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled. Its position is controlled by the integrated air system controllers.

The trim air valves deliver hot air flow to the cockpit and cabin distribution ducts to achieve the temperature requirements of these areas. They are electrically controlled and operated by the integrated air system controllers. If electrical power is lost, they remain in their current position.
Trim air valves remain in their current position.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) includes two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPC), one stick pusher integrated in AP pitch servo, and two stick shakers.
There are two Stall Protection Computers (SPCs). They complete independent computations, and each can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition.
Each Stall Protection Computer (SPC) can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition.
Each control column has one stick shaker, and each Stall Protection Computer (SPC) can drive both stick shakers simultaneously.
The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) commands the AP pitch servo motor to activate the stick pusher. Only when both SPCs generate stick pusher commands simultaneously does the stick pusher activate.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) calculates the AOA threshold for stall alert, stall protection and automatic ignition based on the following inputs: Angle of Attack (AOA), FLAP angle, Airspeed/Mach number, Normal overload, side overload, Ice signal, WING A/I Switch signal, STALL ADVANCE Switch, and WOW Signal.
If the Air Data Computer (ADC) or the Inertial Reference Unit (IRU) data are not available, the Stall Protection System (SPS) uses the data provided by the Integrated Standby Instrument (ISI).

When the current AOA of the aircraft reaches a threshold value, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will generate a stall alert, stall shaker and pusher commands as well as auto-ignition control signals.

The stick-push commands are sent to the autoflight system by the IPC which controls the pitch servo to drive the elevator. Only when both SPC's generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.

fter adjustment through the two flow control valves and two PACKs, the bleed air enters the mixing manifold where it is mixed with recirculated air. If slats fail when extended at or below 10°, the maximum flap extension is limited to 25°.

When the aircraft is on the ground and the airspeed is less than 50 kt, flaps and slats are not restricted by the interlock logic, and they move independently.
Skew sensors monitor the alignment of flaps or slats on the same wing.
The Flap/Slat Electronic Control Unit (FSECU) compares and monitors the position sensors of flaps and slats on both wings to detect asymmetrical alignment.
If the system detects flap/slat skew or asymmetry, the Power Drive Units (PDUs) stop operating, and the system is cut out and locked.

Responses: The main functions of TCAS are to detect aircraft in its vicinity equipped with transponders, display potential and predicted collision targets, and issue vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflicts. It is independent of ground-based ATC and can display up to 30 aircraft simultaneously.
TCAS is independent of ground-based ATC.
The TCAS detection capability is limited to intruders flying within a maximum lateral range of 30 NM to 40 NM and within a maximum altitude range of 9900 ft (9900 ft above/below the aircraft).
up to 30 aircraft
One TCAS receiver/transmitter, Two TCAS directional antennas.
TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders and determines for each intruder its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude.
Its relative bearing, its range and closure rate, and its relative altitude.
Then the TCAS computes the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA.
When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered.
The different classifications of intruders in TCAS are Proximate traffic, Traffic Advisory (TA), Resolution Advisory (RA), and Other Traffic.
Proximate traffic is identified as traffic in the vicinity, closer than 6 NM laterally and ± 1200 ft vertically. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as a filled cyan diamond.
Traffic Advisory (TA) indicates a potential collision threat with a TAU of about 40 seconds. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as a filled amber circle, accompanied by aural messages.
Traffic Advisory (TA) is displayed on the PFD/MFD as a filled amber circle, and it is accompanied by aural messages.

Resolution Advisory (RA) indicates a real collision threat with a TAU of about 25 seconds. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as a filled red box, accompanied by aural messages and vertical speed orders on the PFD.

Resolution Advisory (RA) is displayed on the PFD/MFD as a filled red box, accompanied by aural messages and vertical speed orders on the PFD. It indicates a real collision threat with a TAU of about 25 seconds.
Preventive resolution advisory (PRA) and corrective resolution advisory (CRA).
Other Traffic is identified as non-proximate traffic within the surveillance envelope, with no collision threat. Its position is optionally displayed on the PFD/MFD as an unfilled cyan diamond.
Traffic Advisory (TA), Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA), and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).
It informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when the conditions change.
The preventive resolution advisory warns the pilot to avoid deviation from the present vertical flight path.
The TCAS determined that maintaining the present path will resolve the threat situation.
The corrective resolution advisory warns the pilot to take actions (such as climb or descent) to avoid threat aggravation.

TCAS alerts will be inhibited below 1100 ft AGL during climb or below 900 ft AGL during descent. They will also be inhibited below 1200 ft AGL during climb or below 1000 ft AGL during descend. For RA descents at 1500 ft/min, they will be inhibited below 1650 ft AGL during climb or below 1450 ft AGL during descend. For accelerated RA descents at 2500 ft/min, they will be inhibited below 1650 ft AGL during climb or below 1450 ft AGL during descend.

There are two modes of pressure refueling: automatic refueling and manual refueling.
The refueling mode is selected using the REFUEL SELECTION Switch on the Refuel/Defuel Control Panel.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to AUTO. The INCR/DECRT Switch is used to set the required refuel quantity. The Refuel Shutoff Valve is manually selected open to start refueling. The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the refueling process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when the fuel in the tank reaches the preselected quantity. The FQC automatically records the last preselected refuel quantity and shows it on the refuel/defuel indicator. To activate the FQC for automatic refueling, the INCR/DECRT Switch must be operated, even if the required quantity matches the displayed value. This mode ensures fuel quantities between the left and right fuel tanks are balanced upon completion. Imbalances over 400 kg (882 lb) trigger the FQC to close the shutoff valve in the tank with the higher quantity. When balanced, both valves open to refuel simultaneously. Refueling is completed when the combined total equals the preselected value.

When the fuel quantity is balanced, both refuel shutoff valves are opened to complete the refuel process simultaneously.

Responses: The main components of the air conditioning process include the PACKs, mixing manifold, recirculation fans, trim air system, and emergency RAM air valve.

Bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted through two flow control valves and then processed by two PACKs. Inside the PACKs, bleed air enters a primary heat exchanger, then is compressed, cooled in a main heat exchanger, and further cooled through a reheater/condenser. After passing through a high-pressure water separator and expanding, the cooled air is delivered to the mixing manifold.

The integrated air system controllers (IASCs) control most of these components, including flow control valves, PACKs, trim air pressure regulating valves, trim air valves, and the outflow valve. Recirculation fans are controlled by the RECIRC switch, and cargo shutoff valves are controlled by the CARGO VENT/HEAT switch.
If one Integrated Air System Controller (IASC) fails, the other channel takes over automatically. When one Integrated Air System Controller fails, the alternative starts working automatically.

If both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi. In this situation, sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve.

The emergency RAM air function provides fresh air to the cockpit and cabin when both PACKs fail. It operates by opening an electrically controlled emergency RAM air valve, allowing outside air to enter the mixing manifold. This is only possible if the flight altitude is below 10000 ft and the cabin differential pressure (CAB ΔP) is less than 1 psi. The RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel is used to open this valve.

The emergency RAM air valve can be opened by the flight crew with the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel when both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is below 10000 ft, and the cabin differential pressure (CAB ΔP) is less than 1 psi.
The flight crew can open the emergency RAM air valve with the RAM AIR Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.
The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans and distributes it to the cabin through the distribution duct.
The emergency RAM air valve and low pressure ground connection are both connected to the mixing manifold.
Ground air conditioning source can be supplied through the low pressure ground connection.

Two recirculation fans are used for air recirculation in the cabin. They extract air from the lower side of the cabin, filter it, and send part of it to the mixing manifold to mix with fresh cold air from the PACKs, and the rest to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
Check valves installed on the recirculation fans prevent air backflow.
The recirculation fans are controlled by the RECIRC Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.
Integrated air system controllers can only passively monitor the status of the recirculation fans but not control them.

The trim air system adds hot air to the distribution duct leaving the mixing manifold to adjust the pressure and flow of hot bleed air from the engine or APU, according to the different temperature requirements of the cockpit and cabin, allowing for independent temperature control of these areas.
Manually selecting the TRIM Switch OFF closes the valves, disabling the trim air system.
The trim air pressure regulating valve adjusts air pressure entering the trim air duct from downstream of the flow control valve. When it is closed, the trim air system is inoperative.
The trim air pressure regulating valve is pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled by the integrated air system controllers.

Controlled by the integrated air system controllers, the trim air valves deliver hot air flow to the cockpit and cabin distribution ducts to achieve the temperature requirements of these areas. They are electrically controlled and operated. If electrical power is lost, they remain in their current position.
If electrical power is lost, the trim air valves remain in their current position.

Responses: The Air conditioning system is fully automatic and is controlled and monitored by two Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs). It adjusts bleed air via the PACKs, distributing conditioned air to the cabin, cockpit, avionics compartment, and cargo compartment. Exhaust air is discharged via the outflow valve. An external ground air conditioning unit can supply conditioned air for cabin ventilation when the aircraft is on the ground.
The bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted through two flow control valves and temperature and pressure are adjusted through two PACKs.
The conditioned air is ducted to the cabin, cockpit, avionics compartment and cargo compartment.
The exhaust air is discharged via the outflow valve.
Yes, an external ground air conditioning unit can be used to supply conditioned air to the mixing manifold for cabin ventilation when the aircraft is on the ground.
The bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted through two flow control valves, and temperature and pressure are adjusted through two PACKs.
The bleed air enters the mixing manifold where it is mixed with the recirculated air from the cabin.
Hot trim air from the upstream of the PACK is mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct.
The mixture is distributed to the cockpit and cabin to maintain selected temperature.

On the lower side of the cabin, the air is filtered by recirculation filters and extracted by two recirculation fans. Part of this recirculated air goes to the mixing manifold, while the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
The air conditioning flow is automatically controlled by the integrated air system controllers, which regulate the flow control valves.

The integrated air system controllers regulate the shutoff and overheat protection of bleed air, temperature regulation of the air conditioning system, and flow monitoring by regulating the flow control valves.
The flow control valve is pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled.

When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
The flow control valves can be closed by turning off the L(R) PACK Switch on the AIR CONTROL Panel.

Responses: The AUTOBRAKE Selector is used to select the required deceleration rate for the autobrake system. It has settings for RTO (Runway Takeoff), LO (Low), MED (Medium), HI (High), and OFF.
The autobrake system has two operating modes: landing mode and takeoff mode.
The landing mode is used for the initiation of brake application during landing.
The takeoff mode is used for the initiation of brake application during a rejected takeoff.
During autobrake operation, the system continues to provide antiskid protection, crossover protection and touchdown protection.
ming, Enable and Application.

When the autobrake is set (LO, MED and HI), it is armed in all of the following conditions: The Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight, and The brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake is disarmed after arming in any of the following conditions: The brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals disagree.
The autobrake landing mode is enabled when the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground and the wheel speed is above 60 kt.

Braking starts automatically at the selected deceleration rate when all of the following conditions are met for 3 s: Autobrake is activated, and Both the thrust levers are at IDLE or in the reverser position.

During autobrake application, the autobrake will disarm in any of the following conditions: The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF or RTO. The application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available. The brake system detects a fault. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals disagree. Any thrust lever is pushed forward than IDLE. The ground spoilers are retracted from the extended position.
ming, Enable and Application.

When the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to RTO, the autobrake takeoff mode is armed in all of the following conditions: All Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground. The wheel speed is below 55 kt. The brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake takeoff mode is disarmed after arming in any of the following conditions: The brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO. One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). The Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals received by the wheel brake system disagree.

The autobrake landing mode is enabled when the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground and the wheel speed is above 60 kt. For takeoff mode, it is enabled when the wheel speed is above 60 kt.

The autobrake is disarmed after being enabled if the brake system detects a fault, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO, one or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight, or an "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU) occurs.
The autobrake system operates during application when two thrust levers are in IDLE or reverser position, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is in RTO, and all WOW signals indicate the aircraft is on the ground.

The autobrake will disarm during application in any of the following conditions: The wheel brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO. The application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available. One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight. Any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE.

Responses: Flaps and slats are high lift devices that increase wing lift and decrease stall speed during takeoff, maneuvering, and landing.

Three leading-edge slats and two trailing-edge flap
The flaps and slats are electrically controlled and actuated.
The pilot uses the FLP/SLT Handle or the FLP/SLT OVRD Switch to send a command to the Flap/Slat Electronic Control Unit (FSECU).
The Flap/Slat Electronic Control Units (FSECUs) then send the signals to the Power Drive Units (PDUs) to drive the flaps/slats.
The Flap/Slat Electronic Control Units (FSECUs) receive flap/slat position commands from the FLP/SLT Handle, then send the signals to the Power Drive Units (PDUs) to drive the flaps/slats.
There are two Flap/Slat Electronic Control Units (FSECUs), and each FSECU has independent flap and slat channels.
If one Flap/Slat Electronic Control Unit (FSECU) fails, the flaps/slats will extend and retract at half speed.
If the RAT is the only electrical power source, only one flap/slat channel is powered causing the flaps/slats to operate at half speed.

The FLP/SLT Handle is lifted from its current detent, and the pilot selects a new position. This action sends a command to the Flap/Slat Electronic Control Unit (FSECU), which then signals the Power Drive Units (PDUs) to move the flaps and slats.
During retraction, the flaps retract before the slats.

The FLP/SLT OVRD Switch can be used if the FLP/SLT Handle is jammed or unreliable. Setting this switch to the FLP/SLT OVRD position overrides the handle's command and extends the flaps/slats to the FLAP 3 position.
Using the FLP/SLT OVRD Switch, flaps/slats can be extended to the FLAP 3 position, and the EICAS message "FLAP/SLAT OVERRIDE" will be displayed.
The flap/slat interlock function becomes active when the airspeed is 50 knots or higher.
If flaps are not fully retracted, slats will not retract.
If slats fail when extended at or below 10°, the maximum flap extension is limited to 25°.

Yes, when the aircraft is on the ground and the airspeed is less than 50 kt, flaps and slats are not restricted by the interlock logic and move independently.
Skew sensors are used to monitor the alignment of flaps or slats on the same wing.
The Flap/Slat Electronic Control Unit (FSECU) compares and monitors the position sensors of flaps and slats on both wings to detect symmetrical alignment.
If the system detects flap/slat skew or asymmetry, the Power Drive Units (PDUs) stop operating, and the system is cut out and locked.

When the current AOA of the aircraft reaches a threshold value of the stall alert, the stall protection and auto-ignition. The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will generate a stall alert, stall shaker and pusher commands as well as auto-ignition control signals. The stick-push commands will be sent to the autoflight system by the IPC which controls the pitch servo to drive the elevator. Only when both SPC's generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.
The stick shakers will jitter continuously as long as the AOA is above the threshold. They deactivate when the airframe AOA is less than the threshold of the stick shaker decreased by 0.5°.

If the AOA continues to increase beyond the shaker level after the stick shakers are activated, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will automatically send a push command, and the pitch servo will move the control column forward to prevent aircraft stall.
The push command deactivates when the AOA is less than the threshold of the stick shaker decreased by 0.5°.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) has the following modes: Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1, and Normal Mode.
Compared to normal mode, the threshold value for stall alert in other modes decrease.

Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 1, activates in all of the following conditions: Ice detector on either side detects ice. – Wing anti-ice system available. – STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.

Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2, activates in all of the following conditions: Ice detector on either side detects ice. – Wing anti-ice system available. – STALL ADVANCE Switch is released. – WING A/I Switch is pushed.
To exit Ice Advance Mode 2, cycle the STALL ADVANCE Switch when the flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight. The SPS ICE MODE 2 message will disappear from the EICAS display.
Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2 cannot exit automatically.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) enters Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode in any of the following conditions: Flap system fails on FSECU bus, and flap configuration is not in 0. Flap system fails on FSECU bus or slat angle on both sides is not available, and flap configuration is not in 0. The slat angle difference between the two sides is 3° for 5 s, and flap configuration is not in 0.

The wing anti-ice valve controls the hot air flow of the wing anti-ice system.
The wing anti-ice valve is electrically controlled and pneumatically actuated.

The corresponding wing anti-ice valve closes automatically in any of the following conditions: Loss of electric power, upstream pressure drops below 11.6 psi, or when the ANTI-ICE AIR SOURCE Selector is set to the opposite side.

The Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs) release pressure through the wing anti-ice valve when pressure builds up in the downstream high pressure line of the Pressure Regulating and Shutoff Valve (PRSOV). This pressure release function is triggered in all of the following conditions: Override either side of thrust lever more than 40°, Both flow control valves are closed, Both wing anti-ice valves are closed, Both ENG BLEED AIR Switches are shut off, Both Pressure Regulating and Shutoff Valves (PRSOVs) are closed, Not in the maximum takeoff (APR) thrust, Not in the one-side engine start status.
The pilot can manually select either side or both sides of the engine bleed air from upstream of the wing anti-ice valves through the ANTI-ICE AIR SOURCE Selector.

Responses: To close the sliding window, pull the pull rod, then open the open-lock. Apply the inverted sequence for opening.

The EICAS display (ED) shows engine indications, aircraft system status, and CAS messages.
